claims.text: A 90-year-old man with a history of aspiration pneumonia and Parkinson’s disease had PRG for dysphagia three weeks before an outpatient visit for possible gastrostomy site infection. Initial ultrasound/fluoroscopic mapping, local 2% lidocaine, a single T-fastener, gastric puncture 1 cm from gastropexy and tract dilation preceded insertion of a 14-Fr Entuit balloon catheter through a 16-Fr introducer. Its balloon was inflated with 7 mL sterile distilled water; no additional tagging sutures were applied and the anchor was removed after seven days. At presentation the site was mildly tender, the balloon palpable and approximately half exposed. Abdominal CT showed abdominal-wall embedding and catheter dislodgement from the stomach, without abscess or localized peritonitis. Removal in IR left a large dead space and skin defect too extensive for sutures alone. An 18-Fr catheter was inserted through the existing tract in the operating room, followed by wound debridement and closure. A month of unspecified antibiotics treated inflammation; the site progressively healed without recurrent infection or leakage. At the reported three-month follow-up the wound was fully epithelialized and feeding through the replacement tube continued uneventfully. Initial infection concern remains provisional; antibiotic treatment does not establish a pathogen.

claims.text: An 83-year-old man with hypoxic brain damage underwent PRG for aspiration prevention. Image-guided 18-gauge puncture, a single T-fastener, a 0.035-inch stiff guidewire and tract dilation enabled placement of a 12 Fr Entuit balloon catheter through a 16 Fr introducer. The balloon held 7 mL sterile water and an external bolster secured the catheter. After seven days the anchor was removed and he was discharged without routine follow-up scheduling. Three months after initial PRG he presented with leakage; four days earlier accidental dislodgement had prompted replacement with a 16 Fr balloon catheter. Examination showed erythema/odor. Fluoroscopy and cone-beam CT demonstrated the balloon in the abdominal-wall tract, with the tip barely in the stomach. A post-deflation tubogram showed contrast pooling in dead space. A 24 Fr balloon catheter replaced the prior tube to address leakage from the widened tract, and the enlarged skin opening was sutured. He received a month of unspecified antibiotics. After three months oral intake improved enough for gastrostomy catheter removal.
